analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $250 a month per person, $500 per family.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to the Senate health committee in July 2018 with 20 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans, it died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a hard limit into federal law on what people can be made to pay out of pocket for their prescriptions. Starting in 2020, no one in an Affordable Care Act marketplace plan or an employer health plan could be charged more than $250 a month for their drugs ($500 per family), with the limit rising with medical inflation after that. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with expensive prescriptions, especially those on specialty drugs for cancer, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and HIV, who can face co-insurance charges of thousands of dollars a month even after meeting their deductible. Under the bill, their monthly drug bill would be capped, and the cap would cover everyone in marketplace and employer plans, not just seniors on Medicare.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new required protection to ACA plans: beginning with plan years in 2020, prescription drug cost-sharing cannot exceed $250 per month per individual or $500 per family, and after 2020 the cap rises each year with the medical component of the consumer price index.

The same cap applies to group health plans (job-based insurance) by amending the Public Health Service Act to incorporate the drug cost-sharing limit, so workers with employer coverage get the same protection as marketplace customers.

Under current law, plans must cap total annual out-of-pocket costs but there is no separate limit on what a person can be charged for prescription drugs specifically, so a single specialty drug prescription can cost a patient thousands of dollars in a month.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and premium-payers behind group plans would absorb drug costs above the cap, which would put upward pressure on premiums. Because the bill does nothing to lower the underlying list prices drug makers charge, the money flows to drug companies through insurers rather than being reduced at the source.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps what patients pay but leaves drug list prices untouched, so the costs above the cap shift to insurers and premiums rather than any dollar of drug prices coming down; drug companies would keep charging the same prices and could even sell more product now that patients can afford it.
Applying the cap to employer health plans would raise the cost of job-based coverage, and some of that cost would come back to workers in the form of higher premiums or wages held flat.

A monthly cap set high enough to cover the most expensive specialty drugs would raise costs for plans generally, meaning most people who do not use expensive drugs would pay somewhat more in premiums to protect the minority who do.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 1-3% of patients on drugs costing more than $250 a month, this is real, immediate relief at the pharmacy counter, and the inflation-indexed cap is a durable protection rather than a one-time fix. The honest cost is that the bill buys that relief by shifting spending to insurers and premiums instead of negotiating or capping drug prices themselves, which is why it is best understood as insurance reform, not drug price reform. A bill that also lowered the underlying prices would have been better for everyone.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, which never gave it a hearing or a vote, and it died there when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the bill on July 11, 2018, with 16 other Democratic senators joining as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
Twenty senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

The committee took no further action on the bill: there is no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote in the action history, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and drug makers are better off, since the bill died before it could cap patient drug cost-sharing in their plans; patients with high monthly drug bills got no relief from this bill.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 16 other Democratic senators as original cosponsors.

for.name: 20 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all 20 from the Democratic caucus.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, took no action on the bill after it was referred; it received no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, in a Senate where Republicans held the majority and controlled the committee agenda; the bill never advanced past its committee referral.

industries.note: The bill caps only what patients pay, not what drug companies charge, so it would route relief to patients while leaving high list prices in place; patients could afford drugs they previously skipped, which channels more money to the industry through insurers. Any version of relief that does not touch prices entrenches the industry's pricing power.

Plans would have to absorb prescription drug charges above $250 a month per patient, reducing cost-sharing revenue and raising medical-loss costs, which they would pass back through premiums. Their interest in this bill runs against patients with high drug costs.

The cap applies to job-based group health plans, so self-insured and insured employers would face higher claims costs for workers on expensive drugs, but their employees would get predictable drug bills. The cost would partly land back on workers as higher premiums.
